subject: physics

unit.name: System of Particles and Rotational Motion

chapter: System of Particles and Rotational Motion
question_text: The moment of inertia of a flywheel making 300 revolutions per minute is 0.3 kg·m². Find the torque required to bring it to rest in 20 s.

verification.note: Sri Chaitanya IPE Junior Fastrack (Rev. May 2024), Unit 7 SHORT ANSWER 10 (numerical; the book prints the answer 0.471 N·m). The split — ω, α, then τ — is invented and needs a Telangana IPE teacher. Arithmetic hand-checked: ω = 10π rad/s; α = π/2; τ = 0.15π ≈ 0.471 N·m.

recall_prompt: Say the steps you would write for this answer, in order. You can speak in English, in Telugu, or in both.

steps.label: ω from rpm
steps.margin_note: The 2π/60 conversion is where this class of numerical is won or lost. Write it out.
steps.why: One revolution is 2π radians and one minute is 60 seconds — the conversion is nothing but those two facts.
common_mistakes: Using 300 directly as ω, skipping the 2π/60.
steps.memory_tip: 300 rpm is 5 revolutions per second, and 5 × 2π = 10π ≈ 31.4 rad/s.

steps.label: The retardation
lines: The wheel comes to rest in t = 20 s, so
steps.margin_note: Coming to REST means the change in ω is the whole 10π.
steps.why: Uniform retardation is assumed — the rotational twin of v = u − at with v = 0.
common_mistakes: Using α = ω/2t or forgetting the wheel ends at rest.
steps.memory_tip: From 10π down to 0 in 20 s gives α = 10π/20 = π/2 ≈ 1.57 rad/s².

steps.label: The torque
steps.margin_note: Name it a RETARDING torque — direction matters even in a magnitude answer.
steps.why: τ = Iα is the only physics in the problem; the other two steps only prepare its inputs.
common_mistakes: Leaving the answer as 0.15π without evaluating, when the question asks for the torque.

accept: point one five pi newton metre

steps.memory_tip: 0.3 × 1.57 ≈ 0.47 N·m. A small I and a small α must give a small torque.

insider_note: The last step carries 2 of the 4 marks, and the decimal value with its unit, N·m, is what is checked there.
